The group I play with is rather rambunctious and the games are definitely entertaining, even to the few outside perspectives that have been around during our sessions. I've been considering starting to stream the games on twitch and potentially setting up a website built around a (video or maybe just audio, haven't decided) podcast for the game, and maybe a comic series based on the game as well.

Obviously this is a pipe dream that I think a lot of DM's have, but I wanted to gauge interest in these kinds of things from people who love DnD. I don't really watch or listen to DnD podcasts, with the exception of watching a few of the Acquisitions Inc play sessions (just discovered them thanks to this verse... they are hilarious if you haven't seen any of them.)

So, to the point. How many of you actually watch / listen to stuff like this? I know there are a lot of videos of peoples play sessions out there and it's pretty clear that people aren't beating down the gates of Youtube to watch them. It wouldn't be a waste of time if I enjoyed making them, but I would definitely hesitate on taking on this project if I didn't think anyone would appreciate it.
Game Streaming : Do you watch it?

Full Streams:
I think if you don't have any name recognition then it isn't worth trying to air a full stream of a DnD game. The audience will be mostly (if not all) other DnD players and so you would need some very compelling reasons to get anyone on board with following your group. Acquisitions, Inc. has Chris Perkins for name recognition and they cater to the audience whereas a regular game doesn't exactly run that way. This is all without mentioning the enormous time commitment required to keep up with a campaign, which most people would probably rather allot for Game of Thrones.

Podcasts:
Podcasts somewhat take away the time consumption issue (listen while working, running, etc) but otherwise still have the same issues as a full stream regarding entertainment value.

Comics:
Comics are great (my personal favorite right now is Dummies and Dragons) because they only take a few minutes to consume and can very easily fit into someone's routine. They also are based on the best pieces of a session (or campaign, depending on the format) and don't include all the stuff in between.

__

I think if you could come up with a way to compress a session into a few minutes of video then that would be gold (think Vine compilations). It would take some top notch editing though and probably multiple cameras setup during a session.

I agree with your synopsis. I think the biggest barriers, as you pointed out, are name recognition, consumer time constraints, and hardware (cameras and recording equipment).

I was wondering what is more beneficial for gaming, having high mouse-DPI and low game-sensitivity or the other way around. Does it make a difference? What are you using?

Depends on the game. For instance in counter strike most people have an average DPI and then a really low sensitivity. If either is really high you may struggle to play for long periods of time too as it requires more concentration as your effectively having to react faster. Honestly its whatever your comfortable playing at but generally high DPI is best if your used to it.

Theoretically, high DPI with low sensitivity should be better. Basically the sensor on your 8000DPI mouse will report 1 unit of movement at 8000dpi. When you cut it down to say 2000dpi in the mouse software, it will report 1 unit of movement for every 4 units of movement from the sensor. Since gaming mice poll at high frequencies (1000Hz is common) you get a faster response by leaving the DPI as high as possible, as it reports smaller movements rather than waiting for X number of high-res ticks to report. Then in the software the sensitivity acts as a multiplier.

For example, 8000dpi with a sensitivity of 0.25 should be equivalent to 2000dpi with a sensitivity of 1.0x, but since the mouse will report faster (as in, more ticks) in 8000dpi mode it should be better to use that. AFAIK mice only report integers so it can't report 0.5 of a tick movement, but software scaling is free to use floating point to scale the mouse input down.

Higher DPI is not going to make you more accurate, so it's better to maintain a DPI close to what you find comfortable controlling in desktop use and changing your turn sensitivity in-game. That applies mostly to FPS games which have their own sensitivity slider -- with RTS games you should use whatever DPI lets you most accurately control your units within the game. It's also better if you use the default windows mouse settings (it's bad to change the windows sensitivity slider from default), and try to stick to the native dpi steps of your mouse.

So, someone correct me if I'm wrong, but isn't this simply a new way to exploit information gained in the same way as old exploits? From the article:

When the token is obtained, either through a phishing attack or a drive-by exploit,

So basically, it is detailing a new way to steal stuff once you have the user's password? Don't you still need to provide it (i.e. phishing) or click on some shady link to begin with?

I could be wrong, and would like to know how, but this just doesn't seem as big as the story makes it.

You don't need the user's password. If you can get their token (via a phishing or drive-by exploit) then you can preform the man-in-the-cloud attack (the "new" exploit) against the user. There is still work required on the hacker's end (getting the token), but it's easier to get a file than a password.

It's big news in the sense that, the convenience of having the token (so you don't need to log in every time) provides a major loophole in the security of cloud storage, most cloud storage services allow for this, and it seem that the only difficult part is getting the token itself.

Yeah, I get what you're saying, and agree that it is new, but at the root of the thing is the same general attack that has existed for a while, just grabbing something new that exposes something different.

That's true and a good point, that at the root someone needs to use the same general attack we've known about.

I think the key take-away though, is that that the general attack can be focused to one thing... the token file. The attacker knows exactly what they are after and that's all they need to obtain. In addition, for the new exploit they no longer have to sit in the middle of transmission. With the token file, everything is at the attackers convenience - they can upload malware and then go about their day/week/month/year. Eventually, the user accesses their own file and becomes infected.

This also has major implications for businesses, as there could be trade secrets or confidential information stored there (which I know sounds absurd, but more and more businesses are having their employees host files in Box or OneDrive) and the attacker just needs the token to be able to copy any of it.
So the question becomes, when you install an application on andriod and grant it access to your filesystem, does that mean it can then grab your dropbox token?
